lesson.menu_desc: Reading a real incident report and telling a customer what happened and how it was fixed -- past passive
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 22 -- Incident Report: What Happened, and How It Was Fixed
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Patrícia Xavier Lima Iwashita | Lesson 22 -- Incident Report

paras: An incident was detected by the monitoring system at 9:14 in the morning. New tickets from three accounts, including Northwind Logistics, were not created in the dashboard. While the support team was checking the logs, two more reports arrived from other customers. The problem was confirmed at 9:30, and the affected customers were notified fifteen minutes later.

The cause was found in the release of the night before: a small change in the integration stopped the sync between the two systems. A patch was written and tested in a safe environment, and it was applied at 11:40. The service was restored at 11:52, so the outage lasted two hours and thirty-eight minutes. No data was lost, because every file is backed up every night.

A post-mortem was held the next morning with the support and the product teams. Three actions were agreed. First, a new alert was added, so this kind of failure is detected in minutes and not in half an hour. Second, the release process was changed: from now on, every integration change is tested against a real customer sandbox before it is released. Finally, the affected customers were called personally, and a written report was sent to each of them. Maintenance is planned for the first Sunday of every month, and nothing is changed without notice.
reading.source: Adapted for class use from a customer success incident report

gist.prompt: What is the best one-line summary of this report?
choices: It is a request to open a new support ticket for Northwind Logistics.
It says what the outage was, what caused it, how it was fixed, and what was changed so that it is not repeated.
It is a price list for new monitoring software.

items: The problem was reported by a customer before the monitoring system saw it.
An incident was detected by the monitoring system at 9:14; the customer reports arrived while the team was already checking the logs.
The customers were notified before the problem was confirmed.
The problem was confirmed at 9:30, and the affected customers were notified fifteen minutes later.
No data was lost during the outage.
No data was lost, because every file is backed up every night.
After the incident, the way releases are tested was changed.
From now on, every integration change is tested against a real customer sandbox before it is released.
This report gives the exact minutes of the outage. Why does a customer want that number, and not only the word "sorry"?
The report ends with three actions, not with an apology. In your own accounts, what makes a customer trust a report like this?
If you had to send this report to a director in two sentences, which two facts would you keep?

listenings.text: Hi Patrícia, this is David. I am calling about this morning. My team told me that no tickets were created between nine and twelve, and the whole support queue was frozen. I got your email at nine forty-five, so I know you were on it, and I appreciate that. But my director will ask me three questions tomorrow, and I need the answers in writing. First, what exactly happened, and when the problem was detected. Second, how it was fixed, and how long the outage lasted in minutes. And third, what was changed so that this is not repeated next month. Please keep it short and factual. If the report is clear, the conversation is closed and we move on. Talk later.

Hi Patrícia, it is Karen. I read your draft of the Northwind incident report, and it is almost there. Two things before you send it. First, give the times. A customer who is told that the service was restored at eleven fifty-two feels much calmer than a customer who is told that the team worked very hard. Numbers sound like control; adjectives sound like an excuse. Second, do not open with we made a mistake. Write what happened to the service: the sync was stopped, the tickets were not created, the service was restored. Then, at the end, one sentence about what was changed so that it does not happen again. That last sentence is the one the director reads. And remember, an apology is short. One line is enough, and then the facts. You handled this well today. Send it before lunch.
